Opp
OP
noun (Gen-Z slang, drill/hip-hop origin)
Clipping of opposition (or opponent), from Chicago drill rap (early 2010s), where it named rival-gang members; generalized through the 2020s to mean any enemy, hater, or rival — "watch out for the opps."

📖 Biblical Definition

An opp is an enemy. In its drill-rap homeland the word was deadly literal — rival-gang members tracked and named in songs; as it generalized through gaming and school culture it came to mean anyone perceived as against you: the kid who screenshots your messages, the coworker angling for your spot, the hater in the comments. "Opps" thinking carries a whole posture: assume surveillance, assume malice, keep score, trust no one outside the circle. The Christian observation takes the word more seriously than its users do. First, Scripture agrees that the believer HAS enemies — it is not paranoia but sober doctrine: your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about (1 Pet 5:8), and the world is not neutral toward Christ's people. But Scripture assigns the enemies differently: the real opps are the world, the flesh, and the devil — not the image-bearer across the cafeteria. Toward human adversaries the Lord's command is the most counter-cultural sentence ever spoken: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you (Matt 5:44). A generation trained to sort peers into allies and opps is being discipled into tribal paranoia; the disciple instead watches the true adversary and prays for the human one.

📜 Origin & Era

Drill-rap clipping of "opposition": an enemy or hater; generalized to anyone against you. Scripture relocates the enmity — the real adversary is the devil (1 Pet 5:8); the human "opp" is to be loved and prayed for (Matt 5:44).

OPP, n. (Gen-Z slang; Chicago drill origin, early 2010s) An enemy, rival, or hater; originally a rival-gang member, now anyone perceived as against you.

"Watch the opps" — assume surveillance and malice from outsiders.

Carries a posture: keep score, trust only the circle, read neutrality as hostility.

Generalized through gaming, sports, and school culture in the 2020s.

Decode for parents: your teen has a working doctrine of enemies; Scripture has a better one.

📖 Key Scripture

Matt 5:44 — "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;"

1 Pet 5:8 — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:"

Eph 6:12 — "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."

Rom 12:20 — "Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Opps-culture trains tribal paranoia: every outsider a presumed enemy, every slight a war. Scripture is more realistic about enemies and more radical about their treatment — the true adversary is spiritual; the human one is to be loved.

expand to see more

Paranoia as a lifestyle. Opps-thinking assumes a world of total surveillance and zero good faith — a posture forged in actual gang war and now marketed to thirteen-year-olds as ordinary social software. It manufactures the enemies it fears: treat every peer as a potential opp and you will surely acquire some. The proverb knew the mechanism: a man that hath friends must shew himself friendly. Suspicion is not discernment; it is fear wearing discernment's jacket.

The relocated war. The gospel does not tell the young man there is no war; it tells him where the war is. We wrestle not against flesh and blood (Eph 6:12) — the cafeteria rival is not the enemy; the lion walking about is. And toward the human adversary, Christ issues commands no drill track could conceive: love, bless, do good, pray, feed (Matt 5:44; Rom 12:20). The man who obeys them is not soft; he has simply identified the real opp and refuses to do its recruiting.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Clipping of opposition; Chicago drill (early 2010s) for rival-gang members → generalized 2020s slang for any enemy or hater; carries a posture of tribal suspicion.
